title: Macular Corneal Dystrophy (MCD): The Keratan Sulfate Crisis
summary: Macular Corneal Dystrophy is the least common but most severe of the primary stromal dystrophies. Unlike Granular or Lattice, it is Autosomal Recessive and involves systemic dysregulation of Keratan Sulfate sulfation, leading to full-thickness opacification and significant visual morbidity.

branches: Autosomal Recessive Inheritance (Unique among stromal dystrophies)
Systemic metabolic error in Keratan Sulfate (KS) sulfation

sections.title: Etiology & Genetics
sections.content: Caused by mutations in the CHST6 gene (Carbohydrate Sulfotransferase 6) located on Chromosome 16q22. This gene encodes an enzyme responsible for the sulfation of keratan sulfate. Mutations lead to the accumulation of non-sulfated keratan sulfate (a glycosaminoglycan) within keratocytes and the corneal stroma, as well as in the vascular endothelium and Bowman layer.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Symptoms
content: Early onset photophobia (often the first symptom)
Progressive, painless decrease in visual acuity
Recurrent corneal erosions (less frequent than in Lattice/Granular)
Loss of corneal sensitivity (late stage)
Severe visual disability often by age 20-30

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Grayish-white opacities with ill-defined borders
Opacities start centrally and superficial, move deep and peripheral
Diffuse stromal haze between opacities (clear in GCD)
CORNEAL THINNING (unlike other dystrophies which have normal thickness)
Guttae-like changes on the endothelium
Opacities extend to the limbus (no clear zone)

content.explanation: Macular = Alcian blue = Mucopolysaccharides. (Contrast with: Granular = Masson Trichrome = Hyaline; Lattice = Congo Red = Amyloid).

sections.title: Imaging & Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. High-Res Anterior Segment OCT: Shows hyperreflective deposits in all layers, stromal thinning.
2. Pachymetry: Confirms generalized thinning.
3. Confocal Microscopy: Visualizes intracellular deposits in keratocytes and endothelial pleomorphism.
4. Serum Enzyme ELISA: To determine Type I vs Type II (checks antigenic KS levels).

sections.title: Management & Surgical Protocol
content: Step 1: Conservative Management (Early) - UV-protected glasses and lubrication.
Step 2: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) - Effective only for very superficial anterior Type I disease; risk of scarring.
Step 3: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) - Preferred if endothelium is healthy. Note: Keratocytes in the host rim can migrate and cause recurrence.
Step 4: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) - The definitive treatment for full-thickness involvement and endothelial guttae.
Step 5: Post-Op Monitoring - Vigilant follow-up for high risk of recurrence in the donor graft.

sections.title: Red Flags & Clinical Warnings
content: Do not confuse with Granular Dystrophy: MCD involves the stroma between opacities!
Extreme thinning: High risk of perforation during manual DALK dissection.
Early Recurrence: MCD has the highest and earliest recurrence rate in grafts among stromal dystrophies.
Avoid LASIK/PRK: Severe visual outcomes and unpredictable healing.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The only stromal dystrophy that is Autosomal Recessive.
Corneal thinning is pathognomonic for MCD among the classic trio (Lattice, Granular, Macular).
Deposits are both intracellular (in keratocytes) and extracellular.
The defect isn't just in the eye—it's a systemic failure to sulfate keratan sulfate.

sections.title: Prognosis & Outcomes
sections.content: Visual prognosis is guarded. While PKP provides excellent initial results, recurrence in the graft is common within 10-15 years due to host keratocyte migration or systemic enzyme deficiency. Patients typically require surgical intervention much earlier (2nd-3rd decade) than those with GCD or LCD.

content.explanation: T: Thin stroma; L: Limbus involvement (no clear zone); H: Haze between opacities.
